title: WHAT HAPPENED TO THE AMERICAN MILKMAN

scenes.text: You probably remember the sound before anything else. Early in the morning, before the sun was up. The soft hum of a truck engine at the curb. Footsteps on the porch. And then the gentle clink of glass bottles being set down in a metal box beside the front door. The milkman had come.
scenes.caption: THE CLINK OF GLASS

scenes.text: For generations of Americans, the milkman was as much a part of the neighborhood as the mailman. He came two or three times a week, rain or shine, and he knew every family on his route. And then, within a few short years, he was gone. Almost completely. So what happened to the American milkman?
scenes.caption: AND THEN HE WAS GONE

scenes.text: To answer that, we have to go back. To the horse-drawn wagons, to the glass bottles with cream on top, to the little notes left in empty bottles. And then forward, to the supermarket, the refrigerator and the plastic jug. Let's find out what really happened.
scenes.caption: WHAT HAPPENED?

scenes.text: In the early twentieth century, most American homes had no refrigerator. Families kept food cool in an icebox, a wooden cabinet with a block of ice in the top, delivered by the iceman. Milk spoiled in a day or two. So you needed fresh milk often, and the only way to get it was to have it brought to your door.
scenes.caption: BEFORE THE REFRIGERATOR

scenes.text: Dairies in every town ran delivery routes. Early in the century, the milk came in horse-drawn wagons. The horses knew the routes so well that they walked from house to house on their own, stopping at the right gates while the milkman ran the bottles to the porches. Some dairies still used horses into the nineteen forties and fifties.
scenes.caption: THE HORSE KNEW THE ROUTE

scenes.text: The milkman started work in the middle of the night. He loaded his wagon or truck at the dairy around two or three in the morning, so the milk would be on the doorstep before families woke up for breakfast. In the summer, he raced the sun. In the winter, he fought the snow and ice.
scenes.caption: THREE IN THE MORNING

scenes.text: Milk delivery wasn't just about convenience. For a long time, it was about safety. Milk could carry disease, and in the late eighteen hundreds, bad milk sickened and killed many children in the cities. Pasteurization, inspections and sealed bottles slowly changed that, and the local dairy became a name families trusted with their children's health.
scenes.caption: A MATTER OF HEALTH

scenes.text: Every town had its own dairy, sometimes several. They had names like Sunnyside, Meadow Gold, Hillside, or simply the family name of the farmer who started it. Their names were printed on the bottles, the caps, the trucks and the milk boxes. People were loyal to their dairy the way they were loyal to a ball team.
scenes.caption: YOUR DAIRY

scenes.text: After the war, the milkman was at his peak. The new suburbs were full of young families with lots of children, and children drank a lot of milk. In nineteen sixty-three, according to the Department of Agriculture, about thirty percent of the milk Americans bought was still delivered to their homes.
scenes.caption: THIRTY PERCENT DELIVERED

scenes.text: The milk came in heavy glass bottles, sealed with a paper cap or a foil top. Before homogenized milk took over, the cream rose to the top of the bottle and formed a thick, yellow layer. Children fought over who got it. And on cold winter mornings, the milk sometimes froze and pushed the cap right up out of the bottle.
scenes.caption: THE CREAM ON TOP

scenes.text: Each house had an insulated milk box on the porch, often made of galvanized metal with the dairy's name printed on the side. Some newer houses even had a little door built into the wall near the kitchen, called a milk chute, so the milkman could slide the bottles inside without coming in.
scenes.caption: THE MILK BOX

scenes.text: Families didn't place orders online. They left a note in an empty bottle. Two quarts of milk, one pint of cream, a dozen eggs. Or they set a little cardboard dial on the milk box to show what they wanted that day. The milkman read the note, filled the order, and took the empty bottles back to the dairy to be washed and used again.
scenes.caption: A NOTE IN THE BOTTLE

scenes.text: And it wasn't only milk. The milkman also brought butter, eggs, cottage cheese, buttermilk, orange juice, and sometimes bread. In the summer, some dairies sold ice cream from the truck. A milkman's truck was like a small grocery store on wheels, and it came right to your door.
scenes.caption: A STORE ON WHEELS

scenes.text: The trucks were special too. Many milkmen drove standing up, in a boxy delivery truck with sliding doors on both sides, so they could hop out at every house without opening a door. Some of those trucks could be driven from a standing position with a single lever. A good milkman could serve a whole street in a few minutes.
scenes.caption: DRIVING STANDING UP

scenes.text: A single route might have three or four hundred customers. The milkman carried a route book, with every family's name, address and usual order written in pencil, and the amount each one owed. He memorized most of it anyway. Ask an old milkman today, and he can often still tell you who lived at which house on his route.
scenes.caption: THE ROUTE BOOK

scenes.text: The milkman was more than a delivery man. He knew every family on his route. He knew which houses had a new baby and needed more milk. He knew which old widow lived alone, and if her bottles from yesterday were still sitting on the porch, he knocked on the door to make sure she was all right.
scenes.caption: HE KNEW EVERYONE

scenes.text: On Saturdays, the milkman came around to collect. Families paid weekly, in cash, or by leaving money in an envelope in the milk box. If times were hard, many milkmen let a family run a tab until the next payday. They trusted their customers, and their customers trusted them.
scenes.caption: COLLECTION DAY

scenes.text: Children loved him. Some milkmen let the kids ride along in the truck for a few houses, or handed out chips of ice from the cooler on hot summer days. To a five-year-old, the milkman in his white uniform and cap was almost a hero. He came by before anyone else was even awake.
scenes.caption: THE KIDS LOVED HIM

scenes.text: He wore a uniform. White or light gray, with a cap and sometimes a bow tie, and the dairy's name stitched over the pocket. Dairies wanted their milkmen to look clean and trustworthy, because they were bringing food into people's homes. In those days, a clean white uniform said everything about the product.
scenes.caption: THE WHITE UNIFORM

scenes.text: And there were the jokes. For decades, comedians made jokes about the milkman and the lonely housewife, and every child who looked a little different from his brothers got teased about it. The milkmen themselves mostly laughed along. They had heard every joke a thousand times, usually from their own customers.
scenes.caption: THE JOKES

scenes.text: So what happened? The first big change was the refrigerator. By the nineteen fifties, most American homes had an electric refrigerator, and they were getting bigger every year. Milk could now stay fresh for a week or more. Families no longer needed a delivery every other morning. They could buy a week's worth at once.
scenes.caption: 1. THE REFRIGERATOR

scenes.text: The second change was the supermarket. After the war, huge new supermarkets opened in every suburb, with long refrigerated cases full of milk. And because they bought in such enormous quantities, they could sell milk more cheaply than the dairy could deliver it. Many supermarkets sold milk at a very low price just to get customers through the door.
scenes.caption: 2. THE SUPERMARKET

scenes.text: Delivered milk usually cost a few cents more per quart than milk at the store. In nineteen fifty-five, that didn't seem like much. But for a family with four or five children going through two gallons a day, a few cents a quart added up to real money by the end of the month. Mothers did the math.
scenes.caption: A FEW CENTS MORE

scenes.text: The third change was the car. In the old neighborhoods, many families had no car, and walking home from the store with heavy glass bottles was a chore. But in the suburbs, almost every family had a car, and a big trunk. Mother drove to the supermarket once a week and brought home everything at once, milk included.
scenes.caption: 3. THE CAR

scenes.text: The fourth change was the container. Heavy, breakable glass bottles gave way to waxed paper cartons, and later to plastic gallon jugs. They were lighter and cheaper, and they didn't have to be returned. The whole system of collecting, washing and refilling the bottles stopped making sense.
scenes.caption: 4. THE CARTON

scenes.text: And the fifth change was the cost of the milkman himself. Wages went up. Gasoline went up. Delivering a few bottles to each house on a long suburban route cost more and more, and customers didn't want to pay extra. One by one, dairies decided that home delivery was no longer worth it.
scenes.caption: 5. THE COST

scenes.text: Television helped too. Supermarkets and big national brands advertised on television every night, and families started buying the brands they saw on screen. The small local dairy, with its one truck and its friendly milkman, couldn't afford commercials. Slowly, the big brands won.
scenes.caption: THE TELEVISION ADS

scenes.text: The numbers fell fast. About thirty percent of milk was delivered in nineteen sixty-three. By the mid-nineteen seventies, the figure had dropped to well under ten percent. By the start of the twenty-first century, home delivery was less than one percent. In a single generation, a job that had existed for a century almost disappeared.
scenes.caption: THIRTY PERCENT TO ALMOST NOTHING

scenes.text: Many milkmen worked their last routes in the late sixties and seventies. Some took jobs at the dairy plant. Some drove trucks for the supermarkets that had replaced them. Some retired. And many of their customers remember the morning they read the little notice in the milk box saying the route was ending.
scenes.caption: THE LAST ROUTE

scenes.text: Some milkmen held on longer than others. In parts of New England, the Midwest and the countryside, small dairies kept their routes going into the eighties and nineties, serving older customers who refused to give them up. Those last milkmen became local celebrities, written up in the newspaper as the end of an era.
scenes.caption: THE LAST OF THEM

scenes.text: The milk boxes stayed on the porches for years, empty. Some families used them for packages or garden tools. The little milk chutes in the walls were painted over or sealed up. Today, people buying old houses sometimes find one and wonder what that tiny door could possibly have been for.
scenes.caption: THE LITTLE DOOR IN THE WALL

scenes.text: When the milkman disappeared, something else went with him. The idea that a person from your town would come to your home, know your name, and look after your family in small ways. He was part of a whole world of people who came to the door. The iceman, the bread man, the egg man, the doctor making a house call.
scenes.caption: SOMEONE WHO KNEW YOUR NAME

scenes.text: And something about the mornings changed too. There was a rhythm to the day when the milkman came. The clink of the bottles meant the day had begun. Children knew it was almost time for school. Mothers brought the bottles in, still cold and wet, and poured the first glass at the breakfast table.
scenes.caption: THE RHYTHM OF THE MORNING

scenes.text: Strangely, some of the milkman's ideas are back. Today, people order groceries online and have them left at the door. A few small dairies have even started delivering milk in glass bottles again, for families who want the old way. But it isn't quite the same. The man in the white cap knew who you were.
scenes.caption: IT ISN'T THE SAME

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Do you remember your milkman? What was his name, and what dairy did he drive for? We read every comment. And stay with us, because tomorrow we're going to tackle the biggest myths about nineteen fifties America. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: DO YOU REMEMBER YOUR MILKMAN?
